summary: Follow-up to RFC 392, which reported measurements of network use at Utah. The author says that RFC was meant to point out places the network could improve, not to simply criticise it, and hopes more measurement experiments will be done on other computers and operating systems.

eli5.summary: Someone measured how well the network worked and people took it as a complaint. He explains he only wanted it fixed and wants others to take measurements too.

questions: how fast was the arpanet in 1973
subtitle: Follow-up on network host performance measurements

tldr.problem: RFC 392 reported performance problems with network file transfers, but the message was misinterpreted as criticism rather than a call for improvement.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reframes the earlier findings and reports that BBN optimized the performance, achieving about 400 percent improvement and showing the network itself is efficient when software is well-written.
tldr.outcome: The RFC emphasizes that network performance depends heavily on implementation quality and urges more sites to measure their own performance and share results.

today: RFC 557 is a historical measurement report from 1973 showing that early ARPANET performance could be substantially improved through careful implementation.

sections.title: Clarifying the Original Measurement Report
sections.content: RFC 392 published network performance measurements from the University of Utah that found poor transfer speeds: 75 to 85 seconds of CPU time per megabit (approximately ten dollars per megabit). The RFC author clarifies that the intent was not to criticize the network as broken, but to identify areas for improvement. However, the message was largely received as criticism rather than a call for optimization work.
sections.eli5: An earlier report showed bad network numbers and everyone thought that meant the network was bad. The author wanted to say the network could be better, not that it was broken.

sections.title: Results After Optimization
sections.content: BBN subsequently improved the TENEX host implementation significantly. By updating code to take advantage of recent TENEX changes, improving input/output handling, and using faster network monitor code, they achieved approximately 400 percent performance improvement: from 75 to 85 seconds per megabit down to 19 seconds per megabit (about two dollars and fifty cents per megabit). Of these 19 seconds, 13 seconds were spent in the application program (RJS) and 6 in the TENEX operating system. The 6 seconds in TENEX aligns well with separate FTP measurements at 8.2 CPU seconds per megabit, and improves further to 0.33 cents per megabit when using 32 or 36-bit bytes instead of 8-bit bytes.
sections.eli5: The team rewrote the software and made it four times faster. Some of the slowness was the application program, some was the operating system, and it got even better when using bigger data chunks.

sections.title: The Network Is Efficient
sections.content: The results demonstrate that the ARPANET and its host software, including the host cost, are intrinsically efficient. Poor measured performance stems from careless implementation rather than fundamental network inefficiency. The author urges all sites to measure their own network transfer performance and share results, whether favorable or not. This benchmarking culture would help identify where optimization effort is needed and prevent unsupported claims about network quality.
sections.eli5: The network is actually fast. If transfers are slow, it means your code is slow. Everyone should measure their own results so we know where to fix things.
